**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2026. Paper 2: Section A - Composition; Section B - Prescribed Texts; Section C - Creative Writing. Duration: two hours fifteen minutes.**

Instructions to candidates: ANSWER ONE QUESTION FROM EACH SECTION. ALL QUESTIONS CARRY EQUAL MARKS.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised answer will earn you little or no marks.

**SECTION A - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (10 marks); Expression (8 marks); Accuracy (2 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.enonce_markdown: **c)** Describe an incident of mistaken identity in your community in which there was a violent confrontation between the military and the population. Say what lessons you learned from the incident.
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. Set the scene: day, place, the narrator's age and position.
2. Describe the mistaken identity: who was taken for whom, and why (rumours, plain clothes, same name).
3. Describe the violent confrontation (sights, sounds, injuries, damage).
4. Say how the truth came out and how the conflict ended.
5. State the lessons learned (verify before acting, identify yourself, dialogue before force).

**Model composition (516 words)**

Some days begin like any other and end by changing the way a whole community sees itself. For me, that day was a Saturday in the dry season, when I was fifteen, and the place was the crowded market of our quarter, on the edge of a small town.

It was almost noon. The air was thick with dust, roasting plantains and the shouts of traders. A week earlier, rumours had spread that kidnappers were roaming the area in vehicles, snatching children, and every mother held her child's hand a little tighter. Into this nervous crowd rolled a dusty pick-up truck with mud-covered number plates. It stopped abruptly beside the motorcycle park, and four men in ordinary clothes and caps jumped out. Before anyone could understand what was happening, they seized a young motorbike rider named Tabe and dragged him towards the truck.

"Kidnappers!" a woman screamed. In seconds the word travelled from stall to stall like fire in dry grass. Traders dropped their baskets, young men picked up sticks and stones, and a furious crowd surrounded the truck. Tabe shouted that he had done nothing. One of the strangers raised a card above his head and yelled that they were soldiers, but his voice vanished in the uproar. Someone threw a stone, and it shattered the windscreen.

What followed was terrifying. A shot rang out, then another. People ran in every direction, tables were overturned, tomatoes and cooking oil spread across the ground, and children cried. Within ten minutes a lorry of uniformed soldiers arrived. They fired tear gas, the crowd hurled stones in reply, and for half an hour the market became a battlefield. When the smoke cleared, three soldiers and a dozen villagers were wounded, a boy had a broken arm, and the market lay in ruins.

The truth emerged only in the evening, when our chief and the local pastor persuaded both sides to sit down together. The men had indeed been soldiers in plain clothes, searching for a deserter who had been reported to be using a motorcycle in our area. By an unlucky coincidence, Tabe carried the same name as the wanted man. He was innocent and was released with an apology from the commander. Ours was a double mistake: the soldiers had taken an innocent rider for a fugitive, and we had taken soldiers for kidnappers.

That afternoon taught me lessons I have never forgotten. First, rumour is a dangerous master: fear, once fed with unverified stories, makes honest people see enemies everywhere. Secondly, those who carry authority must identify themselves clearly and work with local leaders, because an arrest carried out in secret looks exactly like a crime. Thirdly, a crowd that acts before it listens can become as dangerous as the evil it fears; a few calm questions would have saved many wounds. Above all, I learnt that dialogue must come before force, on both sides.

Today, whenever I pass the rebuilt market, I remember Tabe's frightened face, and I hope that my community will always stop to ask who someone is before deciding what he deserves.

**Marking grid**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 10 | BOTH tasks are done: a clear description of the incident (mistaken identity AND the confrontation) and a distinct statement of lessons learned; events in logical order, within 500 to 550 words. |
| Expression | 8 | Descriptive and narrative language with sensory details, suspense, a controlled and respectful tone, varied sentences. |
| Accuracy | 2 | Correct tenses (past narrative, present for the lessons today), spelling and punctuation. |

**Common errors**

- Forgetting the second instruction: a good description with no lessons (or lessons only in one line) loses marks for content.
- Using a violent real event with names of real units, officers or places, or taking sides in a political quarrel: the model is a fictional, balanced community story.
